corrections.previousValue:
The airport limousine bus meets your flight and drops you in central Matsue in under an hour. Check in, then head for Matsue Castle — one of only twelve original castle keeps left in Japan, open to 17:00 in October (last entry 16:30). The donjon staircase gets genuinely congested with tour-bus arrivals roughly 10am–3pm; arriving right after opening or from ~16:30 is noticeably calmer, per multiple local visitor accounts.

The Matsue Lake Line loop bus (≈every 30 min, ¥250/ride or ¥700 all-day pass) links the station, the castle, the Horikawa boat dock, Shiomi Nawate, and Matsue Shinjiko Onsen — worth the pass if you'd rather not walk each leg with the group's 2 low-mobility travelers.

Walk the Shiomi Nawate samurai district along the castle moat afterward — low-key, mostly flat, and close enough to the castle that the two low-mobility travelers don't need a second transit leg. Tucked inside it, behind an unassuming long-gate next to the Lafcadio Hearn Old Residence, the small Tanabe Museum of Art is a quieter detour on the same block — ⚠ its posted hours (commonly cited as 9:00–17:00, ¥700, closed Mondays) come from a secondary source, not the museum's own page, so confirm before counting on it. End at Lake Shinji for sunset; it's one of Japan's more reliably photographed sunset spots, a 10-minute walk from most central Matsue hotels.

Dinner: a Shinjiko-shichin (the lake's "seven delicacies" — shijimi clams, whitebait, eel among them) restaurant near the lake. Book ahead for a party of 8; most of these are small, counter-style rooms.

Those two 16:30 cut-offs are the day's one real decision. The castle and the museum stop admitting at the same minute, so you can have the calm late-afternoon castle OR the museum, not both: if the group is checked in and at the castle gate by about 15:00, take the castle first and the museum after; land later than that and take the castle alone, then walk Shiomi Nawate at whatever pace the two slower walkers want. Marching eight people between two 16:30 deadlines on arrival day is exactly the kind of day this trip is meant not to have. End at Lake Shinji for sunset; it's one of Japan's more reliably photographed sunset spots, a 10-minute walk from most central Matsue hotels.

Dinner: Matsu-no-Daidokoro Konekkoya (2F of the Shinjiko Shijimikan, Chidori-cho; 0852-28-7511) for Shinjiko-shichin — the lake's "seven delicacies", shijimi clams, whitebait and eel among them. Dinner service runs 17:00–21:00 with last orders at 20:30, and its 24-seat banquet room is the one nearby room documented to hold all eight of you at one table; courses run ¥3,500 / ¥5,000 / ¥6,000. Phone ahead — the room is shared, not a buyout, and the smaller counter places along the lake can't take a group of 8 at all.
corrections.claim: Tanabe Museum's own visitor page publishes "9時～17時（入館は16時30分迄）", "毎週月曜日（但、祝祭日の場合は開館）", "大人 700円（600円）" with the bracketed rate a 10-person group discount — the ⚠ stood in for a page that was one click away. That 16:30 last admission is the same minute as the castle's, which makes the day's stop order a real choice on an arrival afternoon; and the shipped dinner pick (Konekkoya) publishes address, phone, dinner service 17:00–21:00 (L.O. 20:30) and course prices ¥3,500/5,000/6,000, so "book ahead" can name the place and the number.

corrections.previousValue:
This is the day everything else on the trip is built around. Check out of Matsue with all luggage and take the JR San-in Line to Odashi (45–90 min depending on train) — IC cards stop working at Izumo-shi Station, so have cash or a paper ticket ready before boarding the second leg. From Odashi, the Iwami Kotsu community bus reaches the Iwami Ginzan World Heritage Center in about 30 minutes; drop bags at your Omori lodging first if it's on the way.

Iwami Ginzan is a UNESCO World Heritage silver-mining town — Edo-period merchant houses lining a river valley, with the actual mine tunnel (Ryugenji Mabu) 2.3 km up the valley. Private cars are banned past the park entrance, so the only way in besides walking is the Ginzan Cart: a 6-seat electric shuttle, no reservations, first-come first-served, roughly every 30–40 minutes. With a party of 8 (two with limited walking tolerance), expect to split across two carts or wait one cycle — budget for it rather than assuming the first cart takes everyone. If the cart is full, not running, or the weather's turned, the walk is 2.3 km / ≈45 minutes each way on an unpaved forest trail — a rental e-bike from Daikansho Plaza (¥700/2hr) is a third, confirmed option for anyone who'd rather not wait out a cart cycle or walk the whole way. Local bus service into Omori itself runs on limited frequency — the operator's own guidance is to check the timetable ahead and allow at least half a day for the site.

Head back toward Odashi with real margin: the last convenient upbound JR service toward Matsue leaves Odashi at ≈19:24. Missing it costs a lot more than a wait — the next options are sparse, and Odashi itself has limited late-evening lodging.

Lunch or an afternoon coffee: Gungendo's main store café, a 170-year-old renovated merchant house in the townscape (closed Wednesdays — no conflict today).

Private cars are banned past the park entrance, so the only way in besides walking is the Ginzan Cart: a 6-seat electric shuttle, no reservations, first-come first-served, {{fact:ginzan-cart-500-yen}} depending on where you board. The operator publishes 12–14 runs a day between 8:00 and 18:00 and no fixed interval, so the honest planning number is up to an hour to the next cart, not half an hour. With a party of 8 (two with limited walking tolerance), that means two loads minimum and a second group left standing — decide at the stop who waits and who walks, rather than discovering the split when the cart pulls away with six. Local bus service into Omori itself runs on limited frequency — the operator's own guidance is to check the timetable ahead and allow at least half a day for the site.

The deadline that ends this day is the last bus out of the valley, not a train — you checked out of Matsue this morning and you are sleeping on this side tonight, so nothing here depends on catching a JR service back east. What you can miss is the last Iwami Kotsu bus from Omori / the World Heritage Center toward Ota-shi and your Oda base, and the cart's own 18:00 close is not that deadline. ⚠ Iwami Kotsu revises this timetable seasonally and doesn't publish it on the World Heritage Center's site — ask at the centre's information desk the moment you arrive, and write the last departure down. If it goes: the centre's own transport page lists the Ota-shi taxi firms, Fuji Daiichi Kotsu (0854-82-0660) and Nihon Kotsu's Ota office (0854-82-0456) — a party of 8 is two or three cars, so call before the last bus leaves, not after.

Lunch or an afternoon coffee: Gungendo's main store café, a 170-year-old renovated merchant house in the townscape (closed Wednesdays — no conflict today).

In the village itself, Gungendo's main store — a covered merchant house with its courtyard café — is the dry stop that needs no transit at all. The indoor Iwami Ginzan World Heritage Center is the bigger wet-weather option, but it is NOT at the townscape entrance: the operator puts it about five minutes by road away, so it costs a bus each way and a wait at each end. Check the return time before you commit to it in the rain, or the fallback becomes its own problem.
corrections.claim: The rain plan claimed both fallbacks sit at the townscape entrance with "no extra transit needed"; the operator states "石見銀山世界遺産センターは、大森の町並みから車で５分程度離れた場所にあります" and tells visitors to check the connecting bus timetable — a wet-weather fallback that needs two bus legs must say so.

corrections.previousValue:
Second only to Ise Jingu in Shinto significance, and architecturally distinct — the honden's soaring roofline and the enormous shimenawa (braided straw rope) over the Kaguraden hall are unlike any other shrine on a typical Japan itinerary.

Grounds open 6:00–19:00, free; the rear precinct closes at 16:30 for security. The Treasure Hall (separate building, {{fact:izumo-taisha-treasure-hall-300-yen}} adult) runs 8:30–16:30, last admission 16:00.

Worship here is two bows, four claps, one bow — not the two-clap pattern used almost everywhere else in Japan.

corrections.previousValue:
Omori was one of the world's largest silver-mining towns in the 16th–17th centuries; the preserved merchant houses along the valley road still have people living in them. The actual mine tunnel, Ryugenji Mabu, sits 2.3 km up-valley and is open for walk-through visits along a ≈400m lit stretch.

Private cars are banned past the park entrance — get there by the no-reservation Ginzan Cart (6 seats, roughly every 30–40 min, closed Wednesdays) or on foot (≈45 min each way). This bottleneck is the trip's real physical-feasibility test for a group of 8: plan for splitting across cart trips, not for everyone boarding the first one.
corrections.correctedValue:
Omori was one of the world's largest silver-mining towns in the 16th–17th centuries; the preserved merchant houses along the valley road still have people living in them. The actual mine tunnel, Ryugenji Mabu, sits 2.3 km up-valley and is open for walk-through visits along a ≈400m lit stretch.

Private cars are banned past the park entrance — get there by the no-reservation Ginzan Cart (6 seats, closed Wednesdays) or on foot (≈45 min each way). The operator publishes a daily run COUNT, not an interval — 12–14 runs across 8:00–18:00 — so treat the next cart as up to an hour away rather than half an hour. That is the trip's real physical-feasibility test for a group of 8: two loads minimum, and the second half of the party can lose most of an hour waiting, which is why this sight owns a whole afternoon rather than a slot.

Note the arrival geography: the Iwami Ginzan World Heritage Center, where the bus from Ota-shi runs, is not in the village — the operator puts it about five minutes by road from the Omori townscape, with another bus leg between the two.

corrections.correctedValue:
Tucked inside Shiomi Nawate next to the Lafcadio Hearn Old Residence, entered through an unassuming long-gate — a lower-profile stop than the castle or the main tourist street despite sitting on the same block. The collection is tea-ceremony ware — scrolls, ceramics, lacquer — gathered across 23 generations by the Tanabe family, tatara ironmasters at Yoshida (now Unnan) since the Muromachi period, which is a straighter line into Shimane's own history than the castle gives you. 310-5 Kitahori-cho, Matsue · 0852-26-2211. Worth folding into the Day 1 walk at no extra transit cost.

The museum's own visitor page gives 9:00–17:00, last admission 16:30, closed Mondays (open when a public holiday falls on one); ¥700 adult, ¥500 high-school/university, free below that. The group discount starts at 10 people, so a party of 8 pays the individual rate — don't wait at the desk expecting otherwise.

⚠ Two catches worth a phone call: the museum swaps the permanent display for special exhibitions, which are priced separately and replace the standing collection entirely, and it doesn't publish a 2026 exhibition calendar online. Also note the 16:30 last admission is the same as the castle's — see Day 1 for which one wins on a late arrival.
corrections.claim: Fetched the museum's own ご利用案内: "9時～17時（入館は16時30分迄）", "毎週月曜日（但、祝祭日の場合は開館）", "大人 700円（600円）大学・高校生 500円（400円）" with the bracketed figures a 10-or-more group rate, and "特別展の場合は別途料金となります"; the collection's provenance from the profile page ("田部家が現在の雲南市吉田町で室町時代から営んでいた「たたら製鉄」", 23 generations of collecting). The ⚠ that shipped stood in for one unfetched page, and the remaining honest gap is the unpublished exhibition calendar.
